question.text: Lime reacts exothermally with water to give ‘<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></math>’ which has low solubility in water. Aqueous solution of ‘<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></math>’ is often used for the test of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>CO</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, a test in which insoluble <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></math> is formed. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></math> is further reacted with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>CO</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> then soluble compound is formed. ‘<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></math>' is

solution.text:

The process is known as slaking of lime and the product is slaked lime. It is an exothermic process.

CaOH2aq solution is known as lime water and used for test of CO2.

CaOH2aq→CO2CaCO3CaCO3+CO2excess+H2O→CaHCO32

Milkiness is due to the formation of calcium carbonate and disappearance of milkiness is due to the formation of calcium bicarbonate.
